I am 73 years old, and I have worked these 3 mu in Quzhou for 55 years. My back is not what it used to be, but I know this land better than I know my own hands. My wife and I are only two people now, so I cannot afford to waste labor or money on things that do not pay. We have a well, which means we can irrigate when the sky refuses to rain, but pumping costs electricity, so I use water only at the moments that truly matter.

My wheat is already in the ground—it was sown last autumn after deep ploughing. At my age, I trust improved wheat varieties that I have seen perform steadily in our North China Plain winters. When the wheat greens up this spring, I will spread nitrogen twice: once at reviving and again at jointing, because splitting the fertilizer gives me better ears and less waste. I will irrigate three times from the well—at green-up, jointing, and grain filling. I will spray twice for weeds and aphids, which always show up in our county. After harvest in early June, I must get the summer maize into the ground as fast as possible; every day of delay costs me yield. I will plant hybrid seed directly into the wheat stubble without tillage—this saves my strength, keeps the soil moisture, and lets me finish in one long morning. For the maize, I will apply fertilizer at planting and top-dress once when the plants are knee-high. I will irrigate twice if the summer rains are thin, especially at tasseling. Two pesticide sprays—one for weeds, one for corn borer—are enough. In a normal year, this land gives me about 450 kg of wheat and 550 kg of maize per mu, which feeds us and leaves some grain to sell.
